Hyatt Credit Cards Compared: Is The Personal Or Business Card Better?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card.
  • In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better.
  • Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:.

According to recent reports, the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:.

If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

In a recent development, the first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

According to recent reports, if you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

It has been revealed that the annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

In a recent development, the math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

So my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a significant spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

According to recent reports, that being stated, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

TSA Demanded United Airlines Suspend A Pilot Over Terror Support, Union Accused Of Resisting, Report States

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim.
  • The upcoming report says the intervention happened last week.
  • Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 upgrade on the reported TSA intervention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim. The upcoming report notes the intervention happened last week. The pilot hasn’t been named. Neither has the terror group he allegedly supported. Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 update on the reported TSA intervention Wagenheim’s earlier report cited two sources saying United knew of up to six additional crew members who’d expressed support for terrorist groups. United’s pilots union spokesman declined to discuss individual cases. He said the Air Line Pilots Association has a professional standards committee and legal team that assess accusations against its ethics code and United’s workplace guidelines. The Pilot Israel Barred Was Already On Leave In October, Israel prohibited flights with Sina Amjadian serving as crew from arriving in the country. Israeli officials confirmed the restriction after receiving allegations that he’d expressed support for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah. But United said he wasn’t currently flying, having been on leave since 2024. He flew Boeing 737s and wasn’t qualified on long haul aircraft. Apparently there was material showing Iranian leadership imagery and mourning civilians killed in strikes. There are claims of Hezbollah support and that there was a video of him kissing the regime’s emblem. United Pilot Celebrated October 7 Rapes And Murders As ‘Bravery’ I first wrote about Ibrahim Mossallam in November 2023, after his Facebook description of the October 7 attack as “resistance by a brave people.” United removed him from service with pay but he was reported back flying. On October 6, 2026, after the flydubai pilot sought to use his plane as a missile to attack Israel, United told me: We have withheld this pilot from service pending an ongoing review. There were also reports that he returned after just a day, and that two colleagues had given up first class seats to monitor him in the cockpit. United subsequently denied both accounts. A reported claimed the union blocked his firing. TSA Can Order A Pilot Out Of The Cockpit It was striking that the reported order came from TSA. It has authority that extends well beyond passenger checkpoints. Under federal law, a TSA determination that a pilot poses, or is suspected of posing, a terrorism or passenger safety threat requires the Federal Aviation Administration to take action against the pilot’s certificate. TSA can request that the action take effect immediately. It can also issue mandatory security directives to airlines. However, it isn’t clear from the report what legal mechanism is claimed to have been used and doesn’t report an FAA certificate action. It says the pilot’s “TSA credential” was revoked and describes that as Known Crewmember access. TSA can require an airline to remove someone’s access, but losing that privilege doesn’t mean losing a pilot’s license. Flydubai Shows Why The Concern Is Real I don’t need to know a pilot’s politics. But I wouldn’t want someone who celebrates the killing of civilians at the controls of my flight. That calls their judgment into question even without evidence they’ve planned an attack themselves. The September 30 flydubai cockpit attack makes the concern concrete. The co-pilot of that flight planned a suicide attack on the Tel Aviv airport, attacking the captain with an axe to take over the aircraft. He had satisfied the licensing, good conduct and security requirements for the job, and those checks had failed to uncover his extremist intentions. The values of the person in control of an aircraft matter. #134248. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1985 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).
  • I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product.
  • Recent findings suggest that admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

Recent findings suggest that admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge issues. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

According to recent reports, ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

According to recent reports, royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

Recent findings suggest that we arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

Industry observers note that I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

Boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

We boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

Sources indicate that royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

Industry observers note that these seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

It has been revealed that so the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an matter. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

At 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

According to recent reports, it was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

In a recent development, just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

The lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

The primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

Sources indicate that at 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

Sources indicate that as we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it indicates some effort.

It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

Sources indicate that to be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

Warning For Families Traveling To California: Latest Booster Seat Law Covers Kids Through Age 15

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I have a California trip coming up with my family.
  • Industry observers note that she could fit the belt in our car at home and need a booster in the SUV we get assigned to, but she’s already aged out of the California law that requires the rental organization to have a child seat for her.
  • In a recent development, gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 435 in October 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I have a California trip coming up with my family. If I hadn’t seen this on Twitter, it wouldn’t have occurred to me that my 8-year-old daughter might need a booster for the ride from the airport. We live in Texas, where she’s aged out of the child seat requirement. Starting January 1, 2027, California will insist on measuring how the belt fits her in the car we actually wind up with from National, Avis or Uber. She could fit the belt in our car at home and need a booster in the SUV we get assigned to, but she’s already aged out of the California law that requires the rental organization to have a child seat for her. We might have to bring one with us just in case. Newly introduced Booster Seat Rules Go Into Effect January 1 Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 435 in October 2025. Through the end of this year, a child 8 or older isn’t required to use a car seat or booster seat. Starting January 1, 2027 the rule becomes that a 15 year old requires a booster seat unless all five of these conditions are met: Their back is all the way against the vehicle seat. Their knees bend over the front edge of the cushion. The shoulder belt sits snugly across the middle of their chest and shoulder, clear of their neck. The lap belt sits as low as it can, touching their thighs. They can keep that position for the whole ride. An 8-year old who meets this can ride with just a belt, while a 15-year old who fails to meet one of these conditions needs a booster. Here’s a demonstration of the fit test: . What Happens At The Rental Counter And The Uber Pickup California’s rental car law requires agencies to have a compliant seat available for rent on request for children under 8. This new law doesn’t change that. I don’t count on rental companies having a car seat for my young son, even where it’s required and I’ve reserved it. If they’re out of seats, or the buckle’s broken in the one they have, my wife or I has to wait at the airport while the other one goes to Target. I wrote about a mother at the Atlanta airport who said the seats Avis rented her for her babies didn’t work. Avis indicates airport availability can be limited. At participating Hertz locations, the AAA rate includes a child seat with an advance reservation, subject to availability. ‘Availability’ is doing a lot of work here. Meanwhile, this also has a huge effect on rideshare (and taxis). They’re not required to have a booster. And if I don’t have one, I’m responsible for violations and the driver can decline the ride without it. Los Angeles and San Francisco do have Uber Car Seat. You reserve it in advance, pay a $10 surcharge and get one. It tops out at 49 inches and 65 pounds. A 50-inch child is too tall for the seat Uber supplies and can still need a booster for that ride. And a family with two kids who need restraints still has to supply the second one (or split up and take two Ubers). California is extreme here, although there are various outlier rules already. The U.K. requires boosters until age 12 or 135 centimeters while Germany is age 12 or 150 centimeters. Is This Really A Safety Issue? When a kid scoots forward because their knees don’t bend over a deep seat, the lap belt can ride up over their belly. The theory of the booster seat is that it helps put the force of a crash on the bones of the pelvis. In a study of 388 children and five vehicles, at least 90% of kids 4 feet 9 or taller fit the belt in the compact car and small SUV. Only 77% fit in the large SUV. A study of Washington state crash records found that over a 13 year period looking at 8-12 year olds, 11% in boosters were injured while 15% were injured wearing belts alone. Researchers calculated a 19% reduction in injury risk with a booster, while 0.3% in each group had an incapacitating injury. The study couldn’t establish a difference between booster and no booster for those serious outcomes. There’s a claim of a 45% reduction in injury risk but that’s from a study of 4- to 8-year olds, and even there it seems there’s no statistically significant reduction in injuries. Probably the best we can say is that there’s a real benefit in crash fatality rates for young children but there’s no data suggesting any benefit for 13- to 15-year-olds, and there’s not even any estimate for California preventing injuries with this new law. Who Wanted This Law? Would it surprise you to learn that this bill was supported by the Juvenile Products Manufacturers Association, which is a lobby group for companies that sell booser seats? I’m not sure how a police officer at a traffic stop is supposed to judge whether a child can hold the belt fit position throughout the entire ride. The base fine for violations is $100 the first time and $250 thereafter plus assessments. And 60% of the fines collected go to local health departments to help buy more booster seats. In Car Seats as Contraception, researchers estimate that women with two children still covered by their state’s car seat mandate were 0.73 percentage points less likely to have a third child that year. Fitting three seats across can mean buying a new car. #134246. Breaking: 5 tips to maximize rewards and avoid debt this holiday shopping season

Breaking: 5 tips to maximize rewards and avoid debt this holiday shopping season

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.
  • But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.
  • Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

Sources indicate that first, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you initiative to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

In a recent development, we suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

In a recent development, no matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers.

According to recent reports, we’re massive fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

According to recent reports, A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Related: Best cash-back credit cards.

Recent findings suggest that paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a strategy to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

In a recent development, another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Recent findings suggest that holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

Related: The best cards to use for Black Friday shopping in 2026.

Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley is the oldest member of Congress at age 93, but he remains sharp and focused.

This month, his office announced that he will not be retiring from the Senate, even though a Democrat will take office as governor in January and have the power to appoint someone if any of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats fall vacant.

John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.

Industry News: Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov.
  • Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of problems even as he appears politically weakened at home.
  • Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of problems even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

It has been revealed that the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

Sources indicate that “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he remarked. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Sources indicate that still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., stated part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

Recent findings suggest that “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump stated Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a major reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, stated Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, stated he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

It has been revealed that “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine remarked. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

Sources indicate that during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

According to recent reports, “Enforcement of the latest rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat noted, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

In a recent development, “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he mentioned. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

Industry observers note that trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the tech giant’s president and CEO. He also remarked he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

Sources indicate that the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

Sources indicate that “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear problems dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the spirit of trying out latest ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.
  • According to recent reports, I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could.
  • It has been revealed that after completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the spirit of trying out latest ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

According to recent reports, I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

It has been revealed that after completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉.

Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

Recent findings suggest that on this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That mentioned, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is presently undergoing some refurbishments.

Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

It has been revealed that speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall L. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge new flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

It has been revealed that if you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding….

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

According to recent reports, the legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My strategy was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

Sources indicate that of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

Sources indicate that of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

Recent findings suggest that I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

Recent findings suggest that for those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

Recent findings suggest that despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical issue, so I didn’t take any pictures.

Recent findings suggest that I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

It has been revealed that I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

Sources indicate that neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

Air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

As for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no glitch.

Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting newly introduced people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

In a recent development, if I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

Sources indicate that over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

Recent findings suggest that after being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?

82% Of Americans Fly Once A Year Or Less—And Don’t Know The Rules

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that last Thanksgiving, if you saw an open aisle seat on Southwest Airlines, you were welcome to take it.
  • According to recent reports, travel rules change!
  • every behavior you see in the airport makes perfect sense when you remember >50% of Americans fly less than once a year— Alexis (@aleozimok) November 25, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that last Thanksgiving, if you saw an open aisle seat on Southwest Airlines, you were welcome to take it. Do exactly what you learned a year ago and this Thanksgiving you’re the guy holding up the aisle because the passenger behind you has a boarding pass for your seat, and you’re getting scolded by a flight attendant. Travel rules change! Boarding at Southwest has changed! You might not even know you’re going to have to pay baggage fees if you don’t travel every year. every behavior you see in the airport makes perfect sense when you remember >50% of Americans fly less than once a year— Alexis (@aleozimok) November 25, 2026 The actual number is higher than this. In YouGov’s November 17–19 poll of 1,092 U.S. adult citizens, 34% said they fly less than once a year, 32% said never and 16% said once a year. That’s 66% who fly less than annually (including never) and 82% who fly once a year or less. Just 34% said they’d flown in the past 12 months and 65% said they hadn’t. Who’s Actually In The Seat Next To You? In 2015, then-American Airlines president Scott Kirby said 87% of American’s customers flew them just once in the previous year and generated about half their revenue. Kirby was explaining why American needed basic economy. For every 100 American adults who flew in 2017, 24 took just one trip, and all 100 averaged 5.3 trips apiece. In the 1970s and 1980s, roughly half the air trips Americans took were for business. Personal trips already accounted for about 70% before the pandemic and 74% in 2025. My line when business travel dried up during the pandemic was that “all airline passengers are Spirit Airlines passengers now.” Mask rules drove most of the reported trouble. Of 5,981 unruly passenger reports the Federal Aviation Administration received in 2021, 4,290 involved masks. But losing the regulars sprinkled through coach mattered too. What It Costs To Go See Family In 1977, before deregulation, 25% of U.S. adults flew that year and 63% had ever flown. I’ve written about how much less work it takes to buy a ticket. Between 1995 and 2025, the average domestic fare fell from $618 to $387 in 2025 dollars, a 37% drop excluding bag and seat fees. Fee-inclusive costs are down, too. In a separate YouGov poll earlier in November, 18% of people with family incomes under $50,000 had flown in the past year, compared with 66% at $100,000 or more. Family travel multiplies the cost of tickets across each person while driving costs are constant. AAA expects 72.9 million Americans to drive this Thanksgiving holiday and just under 6 million to fly domestically. Frequent Flyers Share The Same Frustrations With Once A Year Travelers YouGov also asked which things are a major problem with U.S. air travel. Price topped these everyday complaints for both groups. Called this a major problem   Fly less than annually(excludes “never”)   Fly at least annually High fares 64% 66% Delays and cancellations 42% 50% Extra or hidden fees 42% 49% Long security lines 35% 36% But The Travel Experience Is Very Different My status gets me on early enough to find space for my bag. When a flight cancels, I’m looking up alternatives on my phone while I’m in line for an agent. I still have days when I wonder how anybody who does this once a year manages to get where they’re going. A parent buys four tickets and gets a seat map full of prices. Will their eight-year-old sit next to a stranger if they don’t pay? American tells families on one reservation who can’t get seats together that they’re better off skipping seats for everybody than selecting the two they can see. The person who took their laptop out at security on the way there and left it in the bag on the way home may have followed instructions both times. It depends on the scanner in their lane. Say you book a 40 minute connection. You don’t know whether that’s a good idea or not, and may not even know or understand the connecting time, just the departure and arrival times. The airline ends boarding 15 minutes before departure. You’ve got 25 minutes even if you’re on time, some of which you’ll spend getting off the first plane. And if your regional jet on the first segment valet tags your bag, you’re waiting for it on the jet bridge, too. I wound up on Southwest’s first day of assigned seating because American went through three itineraries trying to get me to Washington and I finally bought a ticket to Baltimore. At the gate, Southwest called Group 3 to line up under a sign that still said Group 1. Where, exactly, was the passenger who stopped to read the sign supposed to stand? I’m home this Thanksgiving. I traveled the week before and will travel again the week after. I like to avoid ‘amateur day’. And when I do travel I try to go where other people aren’t. My favorite Thanksgiving trip was Chennai (I wanted to have Thanksgiving dinner with Indians), and I had to explain to CBP on arrival back in the states that we’d done that because it was cheaper booking Lufthansa first class (on points) than going to visit my wife’s family. American tells families on one reservation who can’t get seats together that they’re better off skipping seats for everybody than selecting the two they can see. The person who took their laptop out at security on the way there and left it in the bag on the way home may have followed instructions both times. It depends on the scanner in their lane. Say you book a 40 minute connection. You don’t know whether that’s a good idea or not, and may not even know or understand the connecting time, just the departure and arrival times. The airline ends boarding 15 minutes before departure. You’ve got 25 minutes even if you’re on time, some of which you’ll spend getting off the first plane. And if your regional jet on the first segment valet tags your bag, you’re waiting for it on the jet bridge, too. I wound up on Southwest’s first day of assigned seating because American went through three itineraries trying to get me to Washington and I finally bought a ticket to Baltimore. At the gate, Southwest called Group 3 to line up under a sign that still noted Group 1. Where, exactly, was the passenger who stopped to read the sign supposed to stand? I’m home this Thanksgiving. I traveled the week before and will travel again the week after. I like to avoid ‘amateur day’. And when I do travel I try to go where other people aren’t. My favorite Thanksgiving trip was Chennai (I wanted to have Thanksgiving dinner with Indians), and I had to explain to CBP on arrival back in the states that we’d done that because it was cheaper booking Lufthansa first class (on points) than going to visit my wife’s family. In 1977, before deregulation, 25% of U.S. adults flew that year and 63% had ever flown. I’ve written about how much less work it takes to buy a ticket. Between 1995 and 2025, the average domestic fare fell from $618 to $387 in 2025 dollars, a 37% drop excluding bag and seat fees. Fee-inclusive costs are down, too.

In a separate YouGov poll earlier in November, 18% of people with family incomes under $50,000 had flown in the past year, compared with 66% at $100,000 or more. Family travel multiplies the cost of tickets across each person while driving costs are constant. AAA expects 72.9 million Americans to drive this Thanksgiving holiday and just under 6 million to fly domestically.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, so that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger.
  • Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

In a recent development, so that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.

I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir.

I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w.

Sources indicate that I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

Sources indicate that I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”.

Industry observers note that I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their firm.”.

Sources indicate that @AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR.

@AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their company @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL.

He then attacked American’s rebooking lines at Miami Airport. Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

@AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1.

He also has an issue with bathrooms at Miami Airport, which I get, but goodness, he’s repetitive.

Why do you have the most disgusting bathrooms @iflymia.

Why are your bathroom so nasty @iflymia.

Why are your bathroom never clean@iflymia.

Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia.

You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia.

Sources indicate that he then suggested that he’ll fly Delta or United next time, because they can get you where you’re supposed to go. Yeah, sure bro, they’ll get you out of Miami Airport when it’s closed due to an accident.

In a recent development, next time I'll fly @united or @Delta because they can actually get you where you are supposed to be when you are supposed to be there…and paid for…unlike the incompetent airline @AmericanAir. I bet your life is full of incompetence.

He’s also asking Secretary Duffy to investigate American, because “they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America.” We know the Trump administration loves to investigate corruption, I’m sure they’ll get right on that!

Can you investigate @AmericanAir they are the most unethical and corrupt manufacturer in America.

Honestly, I think American is perfectly justified in banning this guy. He’s violating the manufacturer’s policy on photographing employees, and this kind of behavior doesn’t need to be tolerated.

Recent findings suggest that it sucks when things go wrong while flying, especially for travel around the holidays. But there’s a fine line between a reasonable complaint, and one that’s completely uncalled for. Posting pictures of random pilots and suggesting they’re the reason you can’t see your family for Thanksgiving is not acceptable.

According to recent reports, what’s even worse is when people explain that crew rest requirements are federally mandated, but you just remain in denial over that, and double down. American, please do everyone else a favor and ban this guy.

#134238. Why Austin’s Airport Is Packed While Others Feel Empty—It’s Not Just About Number Of Gates

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 36m • 📚 Deep Dive (7250 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

Why Austin’s Airport Is Packed While Others Feel Empty—It’s Not Just About Number Of Gates

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 36 min read (7250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

⏱️ ~36 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that austin’s airport can be so crowded that you can barely move through the terminal.
  • Recent findings suggest that adam Nathan put together an interesting comparison of passengers per airport gate.
  • For instance, Nathan flags that Austin reduced its gates this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that austin’s airport can be so crowded that you can barely move through the terminal. Passengers spill out of gate areas into the corridor, where everyone else is trying to get somewhere. Then you visit another airport, walk through an almost empty concourse, and wonder why we’re spending billions building more gates there. Adam Nathan put together an interesting comparison of passengers per airport gate. Austin comes out at 637,000, Seattle at 592,000, and Washington Dulles at just 212,000. There’s a lot to learn from this, but the gates aren’t interchangeable, and neither are the conclusions you can draw from them. For instance, Nathan flags that Austin reduced its gates this year. That’s true – it closed its South Terminal with three gates – but those gates handled just 3.6% of the airport’s passengers last year. And Charlotte’s large number of regional jet gates makes average passengers per gate look much more reasonable – when outside of that E concourse, the place is a dense mess. Adam Nathan’s airport passengers-per-gate comparison Austin Closed Gates, But They Were Largely Immaterial Nathan’s slide specifically refers to the South Terminal closure, and that’s fair. Austin closed the separate Allegiant and Frontier facility on March 31, moving those airlines into the main terminal April 1. The site is needed for newly introduced taxiways and the airport’s construction program to grow. However, the airport’s 2025 passenger totals show how lightly those three gates were compared with the main terminal: 2025 traffic South Terminal Main terminal Passengers 771,354 20,895,498 Share of airport passengers 3.6% 96.4% Gates 3 gates 34 gates Annual passengers per gate 257,118 614,573 Frontier carried 553,311 passengers and Allegiant 218,043. Each South Terminal gate handled about 42% as many passengers as a main terminal gate. Moving those flights into an already crowded building wasn’t ideal, but losing three of 37 nominal gates didn’t mean losing 8% of the airport’s passenger capacity. There are actually three different construction stories here: The South Terminal’s three boarding positions went away to make room for work on the airfield. The three new gates at the west end of the main terminal were built to offset gates being taken out for expansion, including the underground connection to the new concourse. Austin is building Concourse M, a separate six-gate facility reached by bus, in addition to the new 26-gate Concourse B. Those six gates will help maintain operations during construction. West Gate Expansion So commenters suggesting “reopen the closed gates” aren’t familiar with the airport. This is space being used to build out the airport. Terminal width matters, too. Boarding lines, arriving passengers and people walking to other gates all compete for the same floor space. Austin’s master proposal identified 89,600 square feet of circulation corridors after the 2019 east expansion, compared with a modeled requirement of 125,350 square feet at 16 million annual passengers and 173,650 at 22 million (almost twice the space). Atlanta’s Concourse D project is a good contrast because it widens the building from 60 feet to 99 feet, increases the depth of gate waiting areas from 20 feet to 35 feet, and reduces the gate count from 40 to 34, with all remaining gates accommodating larger aircraft. Hold passenger traffic constant and passengers per gate rises nearly 18% simply because the denominator shrank—even as passengers get more space. An airport can have fewer gates, higher passengers per gate, and a substantially less density for a better experience walking through the terminal. Charlotte Highlights Why A Low Passenger Count Doesn’t Mean An Idle Gate Charlotte comes out at about 432,000 passengers per gate, well below Austin. If you’ve tried to get through its piers during a connecting bank, that doesn’t describe the experience very well. The airport has an enormous regional operation. It has 45 gates on Concourse E and that concourse handles more aircraft operations per gate than the others. A gate turning regional jets all day can move fewer passengers than a gate with fewer departures on larger aircraft. Charlotte’s planned expansion adds gates and improves aircraft circulation without widening the existing B and C corridors. The ends of the piers at Washington National has the same problem. Why Bigger Planes Don’t Produce The Highest Numbers Flights per gate is a more direct starting point for judging how hard an airline is using its gates. But passengers per gate adds size of aircraft, carrying more people without adding departures. So the surprising part of this comparison is how dense airports with relatively little widebody flying are. But narrowbody gates tend to turn over more frequently. Long haul aircraft often need longer turns, and their schedules are constrained by overnight flying, arrival times and connections at the other end. An international gate can sit empty for hours. And you can’t just replace every regional jet with an Airbus A321. Some routes can’t support it, some passengers value frequency, and some gates and alleyways can’t accommodate it. Upgauging also puts more people into the waiting area for each departure. Dulles Already Has Room To Grow? Washington Dulles is the most provocative comparison because it looks so lightly used while pursuing a roughly $20 billion reconstruction program. I’ve criticized the economics of that plan. First, the slide labels Dulles as having 137 jetbridge gates, excluding 16 remote stands. The airport authority’s 2025 bond documents tell a different story: 121 aircraft parking positions, including regional hardstands without boarding bridges, and excluding 16 remote hardstands. Adding those remote positions produces 137. Since that inventory Concourse E opening November 10 with 14 new gates. Its flexible layout can accommodate a large widebody in space used by two smaller narrowbodies. The number of usable gates actually depends on which planes park there. The same bond documents show 7.3 scheduled departures per gate per day at National versus 3.4 at Dulles for June 2025. The question is how much of that unused time airlines can profitably use. A quiet international concourse at one hour doesn’t establish spare gates where United needs them at another. Nor does it address the 1980s temporary midfield C/D concourse. Replacing outdated buildings, improving train access and getting passengers out of mobile lounges can be worthwhile even without a shortage of gates, although the proposed cost of the project would drive up expenses so much that Dulles could never support a low cost carrier flight again. Analyzing Additional Airports Seattle is working its gates hard. The Port of Seattle’s master plan includes a second terminal with 19 additional gates. Dallas Love Field Is Noticeably Absent This analysis set a threshold of airports with at least 25 gates, so a 20-gate airport serving around 17 million passengers per year gets excluded. That’s roughly 850,000 passengers per gate. Austin leads this sample, not the country. Congress agreed to remove and legally cap gates at the airport as a way of entrenching incumbent positions of American Airlines (limiting competition to their DFW operation) and Southwest (limiting the ability to compete at Love Field) – gates were actually destroyed, in fact six became a Lincoln dealership. Former hubs naturally have leftover capacity. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh were built to handle connecting operations that shrank. Pittsburgh has a reduced 53-gate footprint, rather than its old 75-gate layout. Detroit is lighter use than Atlanta, but that doesn’t mean flights can be re-routed to a different hub. Local demand, fares, geography and the connections already available determine whether shifting a flight makes more or less money. Similarly, San Antonio isn’t interchangeable with Austin, Ontario with Los Angeles, or San Jose with San Francisco. It’s Time To Build—But Users Have To Pay Gates are only one constraint. Runways, weather and available airspace determine how many planes can arrive and depart. Nearby airports may need the same airspace. Taxiway bottlenecks can keep a landed plane from reaching an empty gate. Security, baggage systems, customs and curbs can each run out of capacity too. Austin needs more room for people. Charlotte needs people and airplanes to move through the airport better, wider concourses (and higher ceilings!). Dulles needs to… not do the thing that was declared. And none of this explains why growing airports with millions of customers should get taxpayer money. Airports can issue revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid. I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens.
