    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

    As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

    Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

    The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

    Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s intends to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

    The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

    Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

    Recent findings suggest that “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”.

    In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson mentioned Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”.

    Sources indicate that the DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”.

    Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

    In a recent development, republicans will focus on concerns such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, stated.

    Here are five challenges that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:.

    An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

    Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

    He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

    “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it highlights pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley stated.

    It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

    Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown noted. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”.

    A DOJ spokesperson mentioned “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers mentioned they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”.

    The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

    Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

    On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

    Recent findings suggest that in a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis indicated. Some remarked on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

    Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”.

    Industry observers note that A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation initiative” that would interfere with legal voting.

    In a recent development, last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”.

    In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”.

    Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She mentioned the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”.

    Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”.

    Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

    A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

    “A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” noted David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

    States often change laws and rules related to voting.

    Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

    Sources indicate that A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under latest rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

    Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

    Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two problems involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand newly introduced voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

    Every election features some concerns with voting equipment.

    So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

    In a recent development, ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

    Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

    Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”.

    In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

    Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

    Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, noted the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

    “States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he noted.

    Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

    Industry observers note that late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

    Sources indicate that trump has noted he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The Newly introduced York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

    Industry observers note that nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

    “This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

    In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which noted the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.).

    Sources indicate that some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block latest members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

    Brown stated he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

    “I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown noted.

    Latest Update: Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics.
    • In a recent development, that’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters.
    • In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

    In a recent development, that’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

    In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

    Sources indicate that to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

    These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

    In a recent development, black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

    In a recent development, almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

    According to recent reports, this year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

    They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

    It has been revealed that after 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

    In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a major Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

    In a recent development, louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”.

    In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the massive tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

    Sources indicate that they have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.

    #134211. Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artist’s back catalog with strong results on both sides.
    • Recent findings suggest that “It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record.
    • In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, “You’re Gonna Get It!” Then there’s “Live from the Record Plant,” originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the band’s appearance on the BBC’s “Old Grey Whistle Test,” and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin.” (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artist’s back catalog with strong results on both sides. “Origins 1971-1978” chronicles not just the Heartbreakers’ first two albums but also documents the journey that brought them there, while “The Who By Numbers 50th Anniversary Edition” documents the band’s seventh album in a more traditional box set presentation. Both of the releases successfully accomplish their goals and deliver a worthwhile experience for interested listeners, but follow different paths to reach their respective sonic destinations.

    Recent findings suggest that “It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”.

    In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, “You’re Gonna Get It!” Then there’s “Live from the Record Plant,” originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the band’s appearance on the BBC’s “Old Grey Whistle Test,” and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin.” (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.).

    Recent findings suggest that rounding out the set is a Blu-Ray with hi-res stereo, Dolby Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes, and importantly, a full-color 46-page “fanzine” called “Heart Attack” that serves as the liner notes for this box, with photographs, essays, interviews and commentary from members of the surviving Heartbreakers. There are other editions with additional advanced artifacts like posters or simulated Polaroids — my favorite is probably the “Punk to Upcoming Wave” trading cards — but if you’re in the target market for those kinds of fun treats, you’ve probably already ordered your copy.

    Sources indicate that what’s notable about the unreleased music featured on “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin” is that it isn’t just a simple compilation of demos and rough takes in a logical order of some kind, but instead is deliberately curated into the shape of an album. It’s intended to convey the journey Petty and the band took to get to the place where they’re going into the studio to record that first record, capturing tracks from the Mudcrutch era (Petty’s pre-Heartbreakers band that also featured future Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench) as early as 1971 and then as the Heartbreakers in their early days, learning to work in the studio in L.A. and in Tulsa, where their label Shelter Records sent them to learn how to make a record instead of running the meter on a L.A. studio.

    The outtake record isn’t trying to fabricate something that doesn’t exist or inject fiction into the Heartbreakers legend, but rather, to show you how the band evolved from a bunch of kids in Florida who picked up and went out to L.A. to seek their rock ‘n’ roll fortunes on a wing and a prayer into a band that would end up being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. It’s expanding the legacy, not rewriting history.

    It has been revealed that “It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty, who oversees Petty Legacy, the business concern that’s handling her late father’s catalog, told Salon as she described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”.

    And the collection absolutely burnishes the canon. It’s hard to listen to the selection of music and understand how any music business professional didn’t think this band had serious potential. There’s so many standout tracks: “Parade of Loons,” which opens the record, from the great rock ‘n’ roll tradition of writing a song from the perspective of watching the craziness unfolding around you is borderline fresh wave, but it also isn’t — it’s easy to understand why an industry struggling to understand the new guard needed to figure out where these new guys fit, exactly — and perusing some of the photos included in “Heart Attack” you can extend some grace on that front, because — as Adria Petty laughed, “These are not guys you want to date your daughter, you know?” But as you learn from some of the news clips included in the booklet, Petty did not want to be co-opted into anyone’s movement or limited by any genre.

    “You’re Gonna Learn” is reggae-influenced at a time when that wasn’t a widely known, let alone embraced, genre in American rock, and they manage to pull it off without embarrassing themselves. “Up In Mississippi Tonight” could be an outtake from “Exile on Main Street.” There are also a couple of earnest and successful Dylan homages: “Wild Eyes” and “I Can’t Fight It.” If you’re going to borrow, borrow from the best (and from a guy you’re going to be on the road backing in 10 years).

    Sources indicate that then there’s “Unheard Kind of Hero.” This is a song that Heartbreakers keyboardist Benmont Tench had previously mentioned as a song he saw the band perform before he was in it, and how he was astounded that a band in Gainesville, Florida, was writing original material like that. In “Heart Attack,” Tench offers, “I was following Mudcrutch around because they were so good, and they played a lot of really cool covers and they played some stuff of their own,” he remembers. And when he heard “Hero,” he asked a friend working for the band who sang it originally. When he was told it was an original, his reaction was, “OK, good lord. Because if you listen to that, whether he was 17 or 19 when he wrote it, the storytelling in it is the beginning.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the box set is configured to bring the listener into the story, opening with the outtakes before taking you to the officially released albums, then live radio show and then, finally, the 1977 “Old Grey Whistle Test” performance. But I’d like to make the case that you should begin with the OGWT performance because it is utterly electrifying. Anglophiles are already familiar, but in case you’re not, the “Old Grey Whistle Test” is a legendary BBC music program that was the opposite to “Top of the Pops” in that its focus was on albums as opposed to hit singles. But this isn’t an OGWT where a band plays a couple of songs; this was one of their special editions where the band gets the full show. So this is a 40-minute performance by a band that was already famous and well-liked in the U.K., a status they were still fighting to achieve back home.

    Sources indicate that they’re dressed in black (Benmont Tench rocking a red shirt underneath his suit jacket), Petty looking more like a gunslinger, Ray-Ban aviators and studded guitar strap, Stan Lynch singing harmony vocals over Petty’s shoulder, Mike Campbell dropping guitar riffs and solos without breaking a sweat, Ron Blair sharing the center mic for harmony vocals but otherwise staying low-key back against the drum riser. It’s a time machine back to 1977, with camera work more evolved than we’re used to seeing because it was a TV show about music, not a variety show that featured a band. The colors are a little over-saturated, but people who are used to watching archival rock ‘n’ roll clips won’t be phased. The most jarring element is whenever the camera cuts to the audience, who look like they’d rather be anywhere else. A U.K. source shared that this was because this wasn’t an audience of Tom Petty fans but rather random people who’d put in for tickets and wouldn’t have been encouraged to be enthusiastic. Petty gets his revenge, though, at the last number. (No spoilers!).

    In a recent development, the Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos.

    According to recent reports, “The Who By Numbers” was released in 1975, but this is still being declared a 50th anniversary artifact. It features 92 unreleased audio tracks, a recording of the band live in Swansea in 1976, the requisite Atmos and stereo mixes, and a video of the full concert of The Who at the Silverdome in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1975.

    Also included is what has become a trademark for the band’s reissue sets, a gorgeous full-color 100-page book of liner notes, interviews, lyrics, photographs and other assorted documentation. Even if you buy the CD box, you’re still getting the full-sized book because they put the CDs into an album-sized enclosure. The archivist this time is Andy Neill, one of the two names you want to see behind a Who reissue.

    According to recent reports, the Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos. Townshend was approaching 30 when he began work on the songs for “By Numbers,” and he was in the middle of a number of personal dilemmas, as well as struggling with his and the band’s place within rock ‘n’ roll: “I felt detached from my own songs,” he confesses. He also rued the fact that he felt he owed his best material to the band, instead of being able to pursue more of a solo career, which all of his bandmates had done. Townshend’s “Who Came First” came out in 1972, but there hadn’t been anything since.

    (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) The Who, 1975.

    The demos are lovely, ethereal sketches, documenting Townshend breathing life into his creations for the first time. There are two demos of “Keep Me Turning,” which didn’t make the cut and we wouldn’t hear until it appeared on “Rough Mix,” the warm and affectionate project he recorded with Ronnie Lane of the Faces two years later. A fun game is to take the Townshend demo of “Slip Kid,” where he’s kind of half-speaking, half-singing, and then compare it to Daltrey’s delivery on the finished version, which is the one song from this record that was built on the original demo. (This is a release that you’ll want the good headphones for.) The highlight is probably “How Many Friends,” which is the heartbreaker on the album; Daltrey’s read of it nails the pathos, but this version makes you wish that Pete maybe hung onto it for himself.

    Up next is “Tracking Sessions,” which are initial loose takes with the whole band, but not finished vocals. It’s basically how the band taught themselves the latest material, and it includes listings like “Ramport Jam” where they (sans Keith Moon, still making his way back to the U.K. after hanging out in L.A. and working on his solo record) fart around on a variety of instrumentals and a Faces song. This lasted about half an hour, but we’re getting only eight minutes; given the nature of the release, just give the fans the entire unedited mess. Throughout the sessions, you hear the band members making jokes and laughing; you hear Glyn Johns in the control room offering his thoughts; you hear Pete Townshend complaining about not being able to obtain a suitable breakfast. This stuff is gold.

    Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”.

    There are also lovely early run-throughs of “Imagine A Man” with a solo Townshend on acoustic and Nicky Hopkins on piano, and similarly, “They Are All In Love” (a song that Daltrey did not initially want to sing) is also offered solo Pete. A prototype of “Blue Red and Gray” is here as well, thanks to Glyn Johns’ insistence: “I find that the hardest thing for me to do as a writer is to express optimism, general warmth and a feeling of good will to all men in a song,” Townshend remarked. “It feels trite and I hate it. That song, ‘I Love Every Minute Of The Day’ . . . is a prime example. Glyn Johns wanted it on the album; I cringed when he picked it. He heard it on a cassette and said, ‘What’s that?’ I said, ‘Nothing.’ He said, ‘No. Play it.’ I said, ‘Really, it’s nothing. Just me playing a ukulele.’ But he insisted on doing it. I said, ‘What? That fu*king thing. Here’s me, wanting to commit suicide, and you’re going to put that thing on the record’.”.

    It has been revealed that disc 4 is billed “Early Mixes & Guide Vocals” and is by nature more structured than the Tracking Sessions. The songs are taking shape now. Entwistle offers his approach to his “Success Story,” Pete sings the lead on “However Much I Booze,” there’s a version of “Squeezebox” that the liner notes state is “accented by tambourine” but sounds like the cowbell on the “SNL” “Don’t Fear The Reaper” sketch, and “Dreaming From The Waist” is a fantastic illustration of why Pete Townshend needed Roger Daltrey to sing most of his songs.

    Industry observers note that as a way to track the evolution of the song from start to finish, the inclusion of all of these different versions is an established and useful presentation device, but given their formative nature, it’s not likely that you’re going to go back to them with regularity. But that’s not why this record exists. Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”.

    But it’s probably more accurate to state that “The Who By Numbers” was the record between the “Tommy” movie and “Who Are You,” which isn’t a small distinction; the “Tommy” movie made the band into a larger and different flavor of rock star, one that brought in the girls because of shirtless golden god Daltrey and delivered your average punters who might not have found their way past the tunes they’d heard on the radio. And it’s not unimportant to note that the “Tommy” movie brought the band the kind of money they hadn’t yet seen.

    That’s part of the cri de coeur you hear on “By Numbers.” It’s by no means the main thread, but it absolutely underpins Townshend’s personal anxieties. He’s annoyed that his bandmates are off doing their own thing. He’s perturbed that he doesn’t have the time or material to make another solo record because he has to offer his best songs to The Who (and conversely, it’s kind of hilarious that he then seems panicked when he presented Daltrey with the songs he’d written for the record and ended up shocked that Rog picked “the more personal ones”.) NOTE: Daltrey is not responsible for the abomination that is “Squeeze Box,” that we have to blame on Ronnie Lane, who was enchanted by it.

    The Swansea show from 1976 here isn’t complete, but it is Keith Moon’s last proper show before a U.K. audience. (It was recorded with the intention of being released as a live album, and one of the original tapes went missing at some point in the 1990s, which is why the first two songs are missing.) “My Wife” will sound familiar to anyone who owns the “Maximum RnB” box set, “Squeezebox” is palatable because of Townshend’s giant power chords, “I’m Free” (introduced by Moon, who dedicates it to the occupants of the prison across the street from the venue) sounds more like the version from the “Tommy” soundtrack, and there’s a hilarious comedic bit over “Bellboy.”.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    But it’s the last live artifact here that’s a truly delightful surprise. It’s on the last disc with the Atmos remixes, and at first I feared it would be poor-quality footage added simply because it existed. But it’s far, far better than that. It is the complete show from the Pontiac Silverdome in December of 1975, cleaned up and remastered. This show set the record for the largest ever indoor rock concert attendance of 76,896, which would be broken by Led Zeppelin in the same place two years later. Because of the size of both the venue and the crowd, a large screen was set up to project closed-circuit video, a thing we’d think absolutely nothing of now, but at the time was a revolutionary development.

    There were four cameras, and they do a more than decent job of capturing the action but don’t expect any fancy camerawork or closeups of guitar solos. The sound is in mono — as the liner notes point out, “the sound was captured via a direct line mono feed from the PA — no attempt was made to professionally record the concert for synching purposes.” Part of the “Join Together” / “Road Runner” / “My Generation” medley ended up in “The Kids Are Alright,” but this is the first official release of this footage.

    You know what? The sound quality is more than adequate, and where it falls down the electricity coming off of that stage in this performance makes up for a multitude of sins. Roger is in Woodstock buckskin fringe, and even this primitive setup can capture that those trousers were, shall we say, form-fitting. (Wait for “Magic Bus,” which swings so much harder and better than it did later.) Daltrey introduces the “Tommy” portion by noting, “This is how we used to do it,” and then the band proceeds to light the stage on fire. The band seems perplexed and concerned about the size of the crowd, with both Roger and Pete each taking turns to ask the crowd to take a few steps back.

    This Silverdome footage is absolutely a text, and even this rudimentary capture that was meant to make sure the 76,896th guy in the back could see something is still full of electricity and life. If you were lucky enough to see the band with Keith Moon in those days, you’ll remember, and if you weren’t, this at least brings some of that fairy dust into your life and your house. Put it on, turn it all the way up, and enjoy it without 76,896 people stepping on your feet.

    from music columnist Caryn Rose.

    SEC Proposes Reforms to Shareholder Democracy

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots.
    • According to recent reports, unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades.
    • Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots. Those proposals have become more controversial and divisive over time. The last several years of battles over “woke capitalism” and its inevitable backlash were largely fought through the shareholder resolution process. Now the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is about to rewrite the rules for what makes it onto those shareholder ballots, and that could mean a reset for how politics impacts corporate America — and vice versa.

    According to recent reports, unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades. Originally implemented in 1942 and amended multiple times since, the rule gave the SEC the power to referee which ideas corporate boards need to put up for a vote and which ones they can safely ignore. But the SEC is now proposing to repeal the rule entirely, leaving those decisions up to state governments and individual companies.

    Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    Alec Mena is a research fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    On “SEC Proposes Reforms to Shareholder Democracy”.

    Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Your Questions Answered

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 70 min read (14061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skift

    ⏱️ ~70 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.
    • Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S.
    • The behavior behind it is capital, not talk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Questions from attendees. Answers by Skift Intelligence.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S. airline revenue architecture, and it’s now at the crowded end of its growth curve. Premium cabins generated $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue, in 2024, and U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy. The open question is no longer demand. It’s whether every carrier scaling premium at once dilutes the yields that made it work. 12.

    The behavior behind it is capital, not talk. United ordered more than 250 aircraft with more business class and premium economy, Delta is spending $1 billion on latest Delta One suites arriving in early 2027, American is flying retrofitted 777-300ERs, Alaska is adding business class on widebodies and select narrowbodies plus its first premium economy, and JetBlue is launching domestic first class 345.

    The results follow the spend. Delta’s premium cabins hit 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024, with premium revenue up about 57% over that stretch to $6.9 billion 6. Delta held a 9.5% operating margin through the fuel shock on fares, premium mix, loyalty, and non-flying revenue 7.

    Premium is also being unbundled, which is the clearest sign it has become normal pricing infrastructure rather than a flagship product. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, extending segmentation it already applied to Polaris and Premium Plus 8. United CFO Michael Leskinen mentioned “all of society is becoming more premium,” citing hotels, cruise lines, and car service 9.

    It has been revealed that the front cabin keeps growing but stops being one product. Tiered business fares let carriers sell the seat to price-sensitive buyers without discounting the full experience, which protects yield as capacity rises.

    In a recent development, skift Research’s main caution is oversupply rather than demand weakness. If carriers scale premium simultaneously, especially long-haul, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to trade up and dilute the premium.

    It has been revealed that with jet fuel averaging $4.50 a gallon and domestic fares up about 32% year over year, carriers without premium and loyalty levers are the exposed ones. Deutsche Bank expects American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier to lose money in 2026.

    Sources indicate that premium demand in the U.S. is structural, built on a K-shaped income recovery and self-funded leisure travelers rather than corporate accounts alone. What’s cyclical is the return on it, and that depends on how much premium seating the industry adds from here.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    The U.S. market supports two fully funded premium airlines today — Delta and United — and a contested third seat that American, Alaska, and JetBlue are all spending into at the worst possible moment. Premium demand is real and large, but Skift Research warns the risk ahead is oversupply, not weak demand. Fuel at record levels is deciding who can keep paying for the buildout. 921.

    Premium cabins generate $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue, and Delta drew 50% of passenger revenue from premium in the second quarter 3. United has grown premium seat capacity 46% since 2019, closing on Delta’s lead 5. The economics behind the third seat are much weaker: Deutsche Bank expects Delta, United, Southwest, and Allegiant to be profitable in 2026, while American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier lose money — American and JetBlue by roughly $1 billion pretax each 2.

    Sources: Q3 margins and revenue growth 6; American’s results 1; Alaska’s losses and premium strategy 78; JetBlue’s first class 2.

    Sources indicate that two carriers are monetizing premium; three more are buying the seats and hoping the returns arrive. Skift Research classifies premium as a peaking trend whose main forward risk is yield dilution if everyone scales at once — which is close to what is happening now.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Sources indicate that loyalty cash isn’t going away — Delta took $8.2 billion from Amex in 2025 and Air Canada just had Aeroplan valued at C$10 billion, more than the airline itself. But the economics are less proven than the headline numbers suggest, the regulatory and AI risks are real, and premium cabins are now the faster-growing engine at $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue. 135.

    In a recent development, two things are true at once. The cash from banks is enormous and disclosed; the net profit behind it is not. United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the “credit card manufacturer that happens to fly planes” framing, arguing analysts count what banks pay for miles but ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers — “Nobody counts the cost,” he said 1. Skift’s review of filings found American collected $6.2 billion from card and other partners, while United doesn’t publish total bank cash at all, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 7.2% of passenger miles in 2019 to 10.3% in 2025 1.

    Sources indicate that the clearest structural alternative is premium. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as a peaking trend airlines should scale now, with over 70% of travelers saying they would trade up and Delta’s premium revenue up nearly 50% since 2019 10. American’s Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 6.

    The loyalty engine is being stress-tested from three directions at once: disclosure (nobody shows the net), regulation (uncapped U.S. interchange fees that the Credit Card Competition Act would put at risk), and discovery (AI making fares and benefits easier to compare). None of those kill it. All three argue against treating card remuneration as the only growth story.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    American has closed a lot of product gaps on paper and almost none of the financial ones. Its premium seat mix is already high — roughly 30% of seats generating about 50% of revenue 4 — but Delta converts premium and loyalty into profit at a scale American doesn’t approach 1.

    CEO Robert Isom now calls American a “premium global airline,” a label adopted in press releases in December 2025.

    Premium drove roughly two-thirds of Delta’s passenger-revenue growth, and Delta expects premium revenue to pass main cabin by 2027.

    American’s chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate returns that fund the next round of investment and pay down debt, and that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 2 3. That is the condition American hasn’t met yet.

    American is closing the product gap on a timeline that runs into the early 2030s while Delta compounds the loyalty and margin advantage now. The risk is crowding: with United, Alaska, and most major international carriers expanding premium cabins at once, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to pay up, and yields come under pressure.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    According to recent reports, the premium shift is real and durable, but it is late in its growth, not early. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as “peaking” — a trend to scale now, with oversupply rather than demand weakness as the main risk. It runs as long as capacity discipline holds and the wealth effect behind it holds. The thing that ends it is airlines all expanding the front of the plane at once, diluting yields. 12.

    Industry observers note that the evidence for durability is in the revenue, not the rhetoric. Premium cabins generated $188 billion in 2024, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 1. Delta’s premium cabins reached 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024 3. Air Canada’s premium share has gone from about 20% a decade ago to roughly 30%, with a 35% target by 2030 4. The addressable market widened beyond corporate accounts: Skift Research found more than 70% of travelers say they would trade up, with self-funded leisure travelers driving the growth 1.

    The supply response is where the clock starts. U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy 1. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft 5. Virgin Atlantic is taking refurbished 787s from 192 economy seats to 127 and removing its onboard bars for more premium seats 67. Turkish Airlines is adding premium economy in 2028, leaving Qatar and Etihad among the few long-haul holdouts 3. Alaska is adding premium economy for the first time even after fuel wiped out first-half profit 8.

    Recent findings suggest that unbundling the front cabin keeps yields up without adding seats. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, following Delta, JetBlue, Etihad, Air France, KLM, and Qatar. Air Canada has unbundled business and premium economy and sells legroom in economy.

    ZS’s Kunal Shah said the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

    Premium is now a baseline revenue assumption rather than a stopgap, so the question is no longer whether it lasts but who gets squeezed when everyone’s retrofits land at once. The carriers that survive the dilution will be the ones segmenting inside every cabin instead of just adding seats at the front.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    Sources indicate that no contradiction. American removed international first class from its 777-300ERs to fit 70 Flagship Suites per aircraft — trading a handful of ultra-premium seats for far more business class inventory. The math favors density at the top of the cabin: premium seats are about 30% of American’s fleet and generate roughly 50% of revenue, and premium revenue grew 22.9% in Q3 versus 19.5% in main cabin. 758.

    In a recent development, american confirmed the first class removal back in 2022, framing it then as paying for a 30% increase in premium seats on the 777s and a 63% increase on the 787-9s 8. The retrofitted 777-300ERs now flying carry 70 business class seats 4. International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air Upcoming Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

    Sources indicate that the real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate the returns that fund further improvements and pay down debt 3.

    Eliminating first class is how American funds business class scale — the question is whether a carrier losing money this year can out-invest Delta and United for the same premium travelers.

    The industry is moving the same direction. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft, while reducing first class from 14 suites to 12 6. Virgin Atlantic is replacing its onboard bars with more premium seats 2. Skift Research puts premium cabin revenue at $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 6.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    According to recent reports, tilting schedules toward high-yield local traffic in Upcoming York, Los Angeles, and Chicago is a margin repair, not a differentiator. Those are exactly the markets Delta and United defend hardest, and American is attacking them with the weaker balance sheet. The local-market tilt only differentiates if it is paired with the reliability and premium product American has promised but not yet delivered fleetwide. 12.

    In a recent development, chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that American is tailoring schedules toward higher-yield local markets in Upcoming York, Los Angeles, and Chicago, while leaning on alliance partners to extend global reach 1. Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

    Sources indicate that the local-market tilt is a yield lever American controls, which is why it is being pulled. The uncertainty is whether it can hold corporate and premium local share in three cities where it is the number two or number three carrier, while slowing growth to protect 2027 profitability.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    New York is where the gap between the substantial three is clearest, and Skift’s reporting shows three different postures rather than three comparable expansion programs.

    In a recent development, american’s disclosed JFK plans are schedule and product additions, not a terminal program. Summer 2027 brings JFK–Nice and more Heathrow flying alongside newly introduced Philadelphia and Charlotte transatlantic routes.

    Delta co-financed its own Terminal 4 expansion with the Port Authority’s broader $18.9 billion JFK overhaul, giving it fixed infrastructure control at the airport.

    It has been revealed that united has no JFK slot portfolio of its own. The Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue, cleared by the DOT in July 2025, gives it borrowed access from Terminal 6, plus a net-neutral swap of eight Newark timings.

    It has been revealed that american’s JFK position sits inside a broader catch-up effort. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion, and is on track to lose money in 2026 1. Its Newly introduced York investment is showing up in aircraft and cabins — the A321XLR with 20 Flagship Suites, the 777-300ER with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seating — rather than in gates 21.

    Delta’s advantage is structural. Its Terminal 4 expansion let it consolidate all JFK flying in one facility, within an $18.9 billion airport redevelopment that also produced the new Terminal 1 and Terminal 6 34.

    United’s return is the newest variable. Seven daily round trips is small, but it ends an absence at JFK and comes without United buying slots 5. United’s CFO noted this week that the Blue Sky relationship stops short of a deal, pointing to JetBlue’s nearly $10 billion debt load 6.

    In a recent development, skift’s coverage does not include a disclosed long-term American gate or terminal program at JFK comparable to Delta’s Terminal 4 investment. Treat American’s JFK strategy as route and product-level on the current record.

    This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

    Shares are gross cash from bank partners, not profit.

    Recent findings suggest that allegiant CEO Greg Anderson put the number on the record himself: co-branded credit cards are about 5% of Allegiant’s revenue, against roughly 15% at the legacy carriers and above that at Alaska and Southwest 1. He called closing that gap the airline’s biggest revenue catalyst, with more detail promised at an investor day 1.

    Recent findings suggest that apply that 5% to Allegiant’s actual revenue base and you get the realistic dollar figure. The organization posted $962 million in revenue in the quarter ended July 2026 and $943 million in the prior quarter, a run rate near $3.7 billion including Sun Country, which Allegiant bought for $1.5 billion and closed in May 1. That implies roughly $175 million to $190 million a year in card remuneration. The program had 600,000 cardholders and first-quarter remuneration up 9% 1. For context, Allegiant’s chief marketing officer remarked the Bank of America deal brought in $100 million in 2022, just over 4% of $2.3 billion in revenue 2.

    The structural reason leisure carriers sit at 4% to 6% rather than 15% is spend frequency. Sun Country’s then-CMO estimated a typical customer flies once every 12 to 18 months, which is why discounters pitch the card as a way to stay relevant between trips 8.

    Sources indicate that treat 5% to 7% of total revenue as the realistic planning band for a primarily-leisure U.S. carrier, and 10% to 15% as the legacy ceiling Allegiant is aiming at rather than a near-term forecast. Also note these are gross cash from banks, not margin — United’s Scott Kirby argues analysts count the payments and ignore the cost of carrying award passengers, and no carrier discloses that cost 3.

    This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

    According to recent reports, points stop being a moat once an agent can price them. What holds a member is what an algorithm can’t compare: recognition at the property or gate, reliable operations, and redemption the member can actually get. Skift Research found loyalty affiliation ranked last as a reason to trust an AI recommendation, while 83% of U.S. travelers say better personalization would make them switch programs. 21.

    The pressure is already measurable. Skift Research found 44% of U.S. travelers book outside their preferred program because prices are cheaper elsewhere, and 55% would follow an AI tool to a better deal 1. Among business travelers, consistently good service outranks rewards as a reason to return, 46% to 15%, and 62% say they are likely to switch for a better price or experience 3. Card programs have also taken the top of the rankings: 32% of travelers named credit cards and banks the most rewarding loyalty programs, ahead of hotels at 26% and airlines at 20% 4.

    Industry observers note that the open question is whether recognition and service can be made legible to an agent. Google’s agentic hotel booking passes along only name, payment, occupancy, and property, keeping the conversation that produced the booking — which leaves the differentiators that matter most invisible at the moment of choice. AI referrals still sit below 2% at Booking and Marriott, per Bernstein, so the terms are being set while volume is small.

    This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

    It has been revealed that for airlines, yes — so far. Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23.

    The shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under fresh silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

    The profitability of spend-based status is asserted more often than it is proven. United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    It has been revealed that no cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1.

    U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12.

    Recent findings suggest that where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and mentioned explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

    Sources indicate that the lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

    Industry observers note that nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Sources indicate that neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Substantial Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he says he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15.

    This is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

    Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He mentioned chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

    Industry observers note that jetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

    According to recent reports, the parts of JetBlue’s current blueprint that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

    Recent findings suggest that one caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a latest entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Recent findings suggest that the delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13.

    Sources indicate that the squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

    Breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 showed 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

    Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

    Neeleman said Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

    Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

    Recent findings suggest that the commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Massive Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

    Scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Major Four skip.

    Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

    Neeleman remarked majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

    Recent findings suggest that the practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman said the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

    It has been revealed that the second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

    In a recent development, reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman noted helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

    Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the tech giant’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

    Sources indicate that breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    In a recent development, low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has mentioned directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Big Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13.

    Breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into big cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

    The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    In a recent development, breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12.

    Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and said chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

    Breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman prepares a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its upcoming routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Big Four.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    In a recent development, american can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%.
