The country that right-wing media had spent two years describing as angry, ascendant and permanently realigned voted in an avalanche that crushed years of manufactured MAGA hype. American voters told the president to take his $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks and shove them. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to get away from Democrats and then spent a reported $150 million to deliver the Lone Star State for Republicans, saw his early Tuesday post urging people to vote red disappear from his profile by Wednesday.

    According to recent reports, the country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman governor in American history. Michigan sent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Washington as the first Muslim senator. New Hampshire elected Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man in the Senate. New Mexico made Deb Haaland the first Native American woman governor, and Peggy Flanagan became Minnesota’s first Native American woman senator. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott — the state’s first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Ohio got its first woman governor in Dr. Amy Acton. South Carolina tapped Dr. Annie Andrews as its first elected woman senator. Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in 94 years. While votes are still being counted in key races, solid majorities in both the Senate and House are assured, and Democrats are set to make Hakeem Jeffries the country’s first Black speaker.

    Recent findings suggest that even the Fresh York Post, Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid and a loyal Trump house organ, refused to mince words on its front page: “Trump suffers historic rebuke as Dems romp in midterms,” with “BLUE TSUNAMI” blaring beneath it. On “Fox and Friends” Wednesday morning, Ainsley Earhart warned viewers that “your wallet and your way of life” are now in the crosshairs.

    The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment.

    According to recent reports, it is no surprise that Trump 2.0, stripped of its previous establishment Republican guardrails like Mike Pence and Mitch McConnell, has culminated in such total structural collapse. The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment. Right-wing media spent years confusing its ability to dominate a conversation with its ability to represent a country. When Tuesday’s returns exposed the difference, its leading voices reached for almost everything except accountability. They blamed immigration. They blamed insufficient restrictions on voting. They blamed each other. Alex Jones even decided Trump might secretly be a Democrat.

    For the network’s election night coverage, Fox News seated former Upcoming York Mayor Bill de Blasio between two of Trump’s former press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt, and he told them to their faces that they were “missing the plot.” He said, “The American people are looking at a war they do not believe in, and they did not authorize. They’re looking at prices that are making it impossible for middle-class people, let alone working-class people, to live.”.

    Trump, watching at the White House, raged on Truth Social — “Why does FoxNews have deBlasio” — and seethed at the panel’s lone liberal: “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me.” After Gutfeld read the president’s text on air — which is as good a diagram as exists of what Fox News is now: a suggestion box the president monitors live — Tarlov answered on X, not on Truth Social: “Reality is a tricky thing,” and the president “should get better at dealing with it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on Newsmax, things were somehow worse. Political strategist Dick Morris argued that Trump’s problem was effectively excessive success: He had solved the major problems that would otherwise motivate Republican voters. The influencer ecosystem, meanwhile, went straight for the circular firing squad, and every faction picked a different target.

    Sources indicate that jones, livestreaming as the returns buried his movement, noted Trump himself is the plant: “I think he’s a Democrat. I’m 100% at war with Trump. He’s not that r*tarded. He did this on purpose. I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them.” Benny Johnson and Libs of TikTok reached for the great replacement theory, and Fox’s Lawrence Jones supplied the broadcast version, surveying Texas and concluding, “Texas, there is a lesson here. Don’t be so welcoming.”.

    So much for celebrating people voting with their feet and the U-Hauls leaving California.

    In a recent development, laura Loomer went straight doomer: “America is over and so is the American Dream.” Others blamed Sen. John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE Act and shrink the electorate further, as though the answer to such a broad repudiation were fewer voters. The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro posted the “everything is fine” fire GIF — “Just checking in to see how things are goi—” — and the Federalist’s Sean Davis answered with the hot-dog-suit meme, the one where the man in the costume insists everyone else is the problem.

    At the Races: The upcoming Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Industry observers note that andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews stated, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” noted Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    It has been revealed that “I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Recent findings suggest that peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    In a recent development, A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    Sources indicate that #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Recent findings suggest that rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, declared he intends to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    Industry observers note that RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    In a recent development, where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    Industry observers note that thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Fresh leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    According to recent reports, investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Sources indicate that tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, confirmed a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: Upcoming York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    According to recent reports, after Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    Recent findings suggest that west Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    It has been revealed that monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    #134153. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1214 w)

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.
    • In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.
    • The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their newly introduced congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

    In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

    The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their newly introduced congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

    That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

    Industry observers note that in South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

    It has been revealed that democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

    According to recent reports, democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

    Industry observers note that in Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

    In a recent development, republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the newly introduced lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

    Industry observers note that nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

    After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with latest congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

    Recent findings suggest that with GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

    Recent findings suggest that under less dramatic circumstances, a number of latest faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

    Industry observers note that two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

    Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

    Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

    The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

    Sources indicate that and one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

    Sources indicate that among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in upcoming districts.

    A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

    Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

    Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

    It has been revealed that rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

    Industry observers note that and a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

    This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

The one-time quintessential purple state, a so-goes-the-nation bellwether with a relatively even amount of registered Republicans and Democrats, turned remarkably red in the Trump era following Barack Obamaâs back-to-back wins in 2008 and 2012.     Angie Nixon felt different. The Jacksonville organizer and bookstore owner ran a proudly democratic socialist campaign, advocating for universal healthcare in a state beset by multiple insurance crises and affordability concerns. Ultimately though, Nixon could not replicate the victories of other rabble-rousers like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. The energy in Florida and, remarkably, throughout the South, was with anyone running against Republicans. The blame for Nixonâs defeat lies almost solely with national Democrats and their stubborn refusal to back Nixon with either messaging or money.Â.

    It has been revealed that since her shock primary win in August, Nixon has complained about Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee recalcitrance to anyone who will listen. In September, she told MS NOW hosts Symone Sanders Townsend and Eugene Daniels that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was less than thrilled about her race.

On the other end of the state, typically Republican Jacksonville swung to the left. According to analysis by Wesleyan Media Project, the national party and affiliated PACs spent 10 advertising dollars in Iowa for every one they spent in Florida in the raceâs final weeks, and it demonstrated. The Hawkeye State now has a new Democratic governor-elect and senator-elect.

    It was the same story throughout the South. Democrats overperformed in states where the national party bothered to fight.

We all know that the Colom campaign was locked out of that $30 million contribution to U.S. Senate races,â he remarked. âEven though the money didnât come, in Mississippi, we figure it out.â.

    Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states.
    • According to recent reports, what does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states?
    • The new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Sources indicate that the new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

    According to recent reports, what does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

    The new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

    What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

    Sources indicate that the Horn’s littoral states cannot wish away geography or the incentives that it creates. But they do have room to maneuver. Robust public debate among Horn publics, prudent decision-making from ruling elites, and conscientious engagement from key external partners can ensure that this latest chapter of geopolitical centrality does not further destabilize a region that is already at the precipice.

    It has been revealed that the Horn of Africa has been a critical node since the inauguration of the Suez Canal in 1869. But the intensity with which this fact has been felt has waxed and waned over time. The start of the Yemen War in 2015 initiated another period of growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and a range of outside powers, each of whom sought a strategic perch near the Red Sea corridor from which to project their security and commercial interests.

    But the turmoil in the  Middle East after Oct. 7, 2023, has sharpened this dynamic. Two developments have been particularly consequential. The first is the Houthi campaign to interrupt maritime traffic in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, with a first wave of attacks beginning in November 2023 and a second wave targeting Saudi shipping starting in the summer of 2026. The second dynamic has been the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East. Although these respective blocs are not entirely coherent, there are clear divisions over Israel’s increasingly muscular security policy; the Iran crisis; and their respective interventions in conflicts between national governments and subnational armed actors across the region.

    Industry observers note that in the face of newly introduced strategic pressures, several extra-regional actors have sought enhanced access and position in this zone, over and above what they had secured in preceding years. A triumvirate of littoral countries/de-facto states have been immediate targets: Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea.

    The impact is most apparent in Somaliland. Its economic partnership with the UAE, through the latter’s investment in the Berbera corridor, is long-standing. But this relationship has become increasingly securitized since 2024. The clearest evidence is what transpired at Berbera Airport, which has come under the effective security control of the UAE. Satellite imagery suggests the construction of an adjoining dock and the hardening of the airport’s infrastructure, including the development of underground bunkers that are potentially for ammunition and fuel. Many believe the airport has also become a logistical node in the UAE’s broader military supply network across East Africa, enabling the delivery of weapons to Sudan and Ethiopia.

    Israel’s expanding role in Somaliland has run in parallel with the growing Emirati military presence. Israel diplomatically recognized Somaliland in December 2025—making it the first country in the world to do so—and some reports suggest an active Israeli intelligence presence in Berbera and the use of the airport for refueling its jets during the Iran war. Somaliland officials generally do not confirm these reports but acknowledge that an Israeli military presence is an eventual possibility.

    A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in Hargeisa, Somaliland, on Oct. 16. Mohamed Ahmed/Reuters.

    In a recent development, washington has also joined the club. In the last year, Somaliland has hosted the commanding generals of AFRICOM and SOCAFRICA. A number of U.S. military personnel based at the Baledogle Airfield in Somalia have now been redeployed to Somaliland, prompting one senior Somaliland official to privately quip, “Team Mogadishu has now become Team Hargeisa.” U.S. training opportunities for Somaliland’s security forces appear to have also grown. These developments are still nascent and as such do not yet involve the deployment of critical intelligence, security, and reconnaissance capabilities, but the direction of travel is fairly clear.

    The Emirati government’s formula in Puntland has largely tracked its approach to Somaliland. Beginning in the 2010s, the Emirati footprint in the statelet had mostly consisted of a commercial port concession in Bosaso and training Puntland’s Maritime Security Forces. But from 2024 onward, the UAE scaled up its activity in Bosaso, turning an airbase next to the civilian airport into another logistical hub through which weapons, ammunition, and personnel flowed to Emirati allies throughout the Horn. The UAE has also supported Puntland’s 2024-2025 offensive against Islamic State contingents in the region through direct drone strikes. The United States has also directly backed counter-Islamic State military operations, and according to Puntland authorities, agreed in August 2026 to establish a military facility at the same Bosaso airbase that houses an Emirati presence.

    Industry observers note that eritrea’s incorporation into this picture looks a bit different. Its external alignments sharply diverge from Somaliland and Puntland, and there is currently no evidence that Eritrea is poised to play host to foreign military facilities. Yet if the past is prologue, then Eritrea could soon find itself housing a more significant military presence. There are unconfirmed reports of the potential for an increased Egyptian presence in the southern port of Assab. Assab served as the logistical fulcrum of Emirati military operations in Yemen, and back in the early 2000s, the Eritrean government lobbied the United States to establish a military base in Eritrea. At the time, Washington declined the Eritrean offer and established its premiere African military base in neighboring Djibouti.

    People sail past container ships anchored near the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Aug. 6. AFP via Getty Images.

    Maritime exigencies in and around the Bab el-Mandeb have now pushed Eritrea higher on the Trump administration’s agenda. While U.S.-Eritrea relations have been relatively poor for more than two decades, Washington allowed a Tigray-related sanctions package targeting the Eritrean government to expire in September 2026. This was a clear bid to enhance relations with Asmara and was tied to a broad, if not clearly defined, sense that Eritrea mattered for Red Sea security. This sanctions removal occurred even though some crucial U.S. policymakers believed that Eritrea had not really done enough to warrant such action.

    Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea will probably extract clear strategic rewards from their emerging geopolitical centrality and the related expansion of security partnerships. All three face increasingly acute security dilemmas from what they regard as revanchist neighbors and their respective external backers. All of their national political projects are also at critical junctures: Somaliland is attempting to build momentum for wider recognition; Puntland is maneuvering to protect its autonomy within a Somali federation; and Eritrea is working to fully break its political estrangement from much of the international system. Somaliland and Puntland have even leveraged the good offices of Abu Dhabi and Washington to improve a bilateral relationship long riddled with tension.

    People participate in a rally to celebrate the Houthis’ takeover of the strategic port city of Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb strait in Sana’a, Yemen, on Sept. 11. Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images.

    Recent findings suggest that the risks, however, are very real. The first is that these small polities rapidly find themselves entrapped in conflicts that are not their own. The concern is most relevant to Somaliland, where the intensification of the Emirati, Israeli, and U.S. security presence is clearest. Though Houthi attacks in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have had negative economic repercussions on Berbera port, Somaliland’s authorities have no interest in getting involved in a regional war against the Houthis. But they might not have a choice. The Houthis themselves have threatened to strike any Israeli military presence in Somaliland and even hacked the website of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in early July. If a conflict led to missile or drone strikes on Berbera, it would have a catastrophic impact on trade, government revenue, and oil imports.

    It has been revealed that there is also a risk that Somaliland’s deepening security engagement with the Abraham bloc alienates it from Saudi Arabia, which is clearly unnerved by the growing security presence of the Emiratis and Israelis in the southern Red Sea. Somaliland’s critical livestock export sector, which provides 80 percent of all export earnings, is oriented toward the Saudi market, meaning it can ill afford to antagonize Riyadh.

    Industry observers note that somaliland’s authorities are no doubt hoping to manage the scale and conduct of the foreign military element within its borders, so as to not provoke retaliation from actors they otherwise have few differences with. Although not widely known, when it was negotiating a memorandum of understanding for sea access with Ethiopia in late 2023, Somaliland placed real limitations on an Ethiopian naval presence in its Gulf of Aden shores. This included the denial of a land corridor between the Ethiopian border and naval base, as well as limits on the Ethiopian military’s interactions with local communities and third-party military activity. But does Somaliland have the autonomy to fully constrain what Israel, the UAE, and the United States do within its borders?

    The second risk is that external actors’ push for new Red Sea-oriented partnerships might inadvertently fuel escalatory dynamics in the region. This is most evident in the growing tensions between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The scramble for positions along the Horn’s Red Sea littoral has provided landlocked Ethiopia a new set of justifications to press its maritime claims, including to the port of Assab in Eritrea. Ethiopian officials have argued that since the Red Sea and its Horn ports are increasingly contested terrain, an Ethiopian naval presence is the only way to ensure the country’s economic and security interests. They also make the point that if it is legitimate for outside powers to establish military bases along the Red Sea littoral, then it is an equally legitimate course of action for Ethiopia.

    A view of U.S. military aircraft at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti on Jan. 21, 2024. Djibouti sits opposite Yemen, across the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and between Eritrea and Somaliland.Getty Images.

    At the same time, U.S. sanctions removal, and the growing proximity between Cairo and Asmara, has increased Eritrea’s willingness to risk conflict with its southern neighbor. Indeed, the decision by the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival to launch offensives on Sept. 23, likely with the approval of Asmara, came just six days after the U.S. sanctions regime on Eritrea expired.

    Meanwhile, Emirati-Israeli involvement in Somaliland and Puntland has further consolidated Mogadishu’s increasing all-weather alliance with Turkey. President Hassan Sheikh has used Somalia’s growing defense partnerships with Turkey, which has deployed F-16s to the region to fight Al-Shabaab, to put pressure on Somaliland and Puntland. Most recently, this has involved an electronic visa scheme managed by Mogadishu to control the movement of foreign passport holders into Somaliland, and a reported agreement with Ankara to build a military base in Laasqoray, which sits in territory that Somaliland considers its own.

    Analysts fear that the renewed conflict could quickly draw in other regional actors.

    How Washington bargains away its Africa strategy to other regions.

    It has been revealed that as a result, the risk of conflict between Mogadishu, Garowe, and even Hargeisa has increased considerably. In July and August, for instance, there were military confrontations between Puntland’s government and the Puntland Security Force, a militia that had increasingly come under the sway of Mogadishu, resulting in the PSF bases in Galkayo and Bosaso being seized by Puntland authorities.

    A final risk is related to the core governance questions that will shape the regional security landscape of the Horn in the coming years.

    Consider Eritrea, which has been mired in a deep human rights crisis for decades. This has driven hundreds of thousands of its young people abroad and produced deep, if still suppressed, social fissures. The country has no functioning constitution or electoral system, and thus no mechanism for peacefully navigating succession or adjudicating domestic political differences. Its political elite, in power since 1991, is unwilling to cultivate younger leaders or embrace basic economic and political reforms, offering little more than time-worn cliches about the need to defend against sabotage by external enemies. Unsurprisingly, U.S. sanctions relief engages none of these concerns.

    Industry observers note that in Somaliland and Puntland, the problem is one of political polarization, as deepening external partnerships have widened disagreements between contending political factions. Somaliland’s recognition deal with Israel has drawn internal criticism, including from religious actors, on both moral and strategic grounds. This was particularly true after Hargeisa made the controversial decision to place its embassy in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv in July. In Puntland, some opponents of President Saeed Deni believe he is using Emirati patronage to further consolidate his power. In all of these debates and more, fairly explosive clan rivalries lurk just beneath the surface.

    Members of the Somaliland Coast Guard participate in a parade in Hargeisa on May 18. Kang-Chun Cheng/AFP via Getty Images.

    Recent findings suggest that the Horn’s littoral states can navigate the risks associated with their emerging geopolitical centrality. But it will require more than business as usual. The first step is robust public debate about the risks and rewards of external security entanglements, so that all relevant considerations are surfaced. In many ways, Somaliland is ahead of the curve in this regard, a reflection of its relatively strong—although far from perfect—democratic system.

    Ruling elites must also prudently assess the costs and benefits of foreign basing and military cooperation. The challenge here is that the democratic deficit in some of these states means that regime security often prevails over public interest. There are also separate questions of state capacity in some of these polities and the fundamental ability of the government to recognize substantive problems and devise responses. Finally, external partners, particularly the United States, must recognize that the transactionalism of the moment will not deliver stability in one of the world’s most essential maritime corridors. The only solution is to encourage better and more accountable governance along Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden littoral.

    Industry observers note that michael Woldemariam is an associate professor and the Ph.D. program director in the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy.

    Biruk Terrefe is a lecturer in African politics at the University of Bayreuth and a research associate at Oxford’s African Studies Centre.

    House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., stated earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    Recent findings suggest that “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., remarked during the meeting.

    Sources indicate that when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” noted panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    Industry observers note that the committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    In a recent development, it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    In a recent development, “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack mentioned that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack remarked in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., remarked everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he remarked at Thursday’s meeting.

    Good Points, Palmer Luckey

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (172 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that at his DealBook interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin last week, Palmer Luckey, founder of AI weapon producer Anduril, made a clear case for the American defense sector, one based on recognizing that our society is protected by physical military power, that America is fundamentally good and deserving of this protection, and that the rest of the world benefits from a muscular (and not necessarily confrontational) America.
    • It’s not often that we hear contentious positions on American strength explained without cartoonish warrior-posturing.
    • Fellow in Political Journalism for National Review.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

    That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

    Sources indicate that waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”.

    Reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”).

    Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

    Industry observers note that not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    In a recent development, one would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

    Recent findings suggest that but this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

    For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a newly introduced project after a string of flops.

    If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person notes so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

    In a recent development, what Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

    But it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    What’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion highlights maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

    If America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

    While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, mentioned additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    In a recent development, as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Sources indicate that democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    Industry observers note that “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    According to recent reports, as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    According to recent reports, last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    According to recent reports, “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, remarked at a news conference.

    In a recent development, sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., noted Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    According to recent reports, the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    Industry News: Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    • Industry observers note that the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    Industry observers note that the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    In a recent development, now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    “It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, mentioned John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”.

    Trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

    In a recent development, “I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” said Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”.

    Recent findings suggest that now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the newly introduced loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

    The European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has noted the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this latest European loan something of a question mark.

    “Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” said Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.).

    It has been revealed that the bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

    “Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst noted.

    Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

    For all the talk of a latest world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

    One question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”.

    Sources indicate that “If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash said.

    “It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”.

    • Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin.

    Gratitude is like stretching, or deep breathing, or drinking water. It’s one of those miraculous things you can do for free, any time, with barely any effort, and it’s 100 percent certain to make you feel better — but somehow practicing it always feels like an exasperating chore. That’s how I experience it, anyway. There comes a moment at nearly all Thanksgiving tables when someone notes, Now let’s all go around and say one thing we’re thankful for. And when this unimpeachably virtuous ritual is unveiled, my first thought is always, Oh God, when will it be over?

    Sources indicate that but then of course — like drinking water, or breathing deeply — giving thanks is also something you’re always glad you did. Lo and behold, there really are people and things you love in this world, and to make a point of looking on them with appreciation is to see them lit up again in the living color of your own happiness. You might start out by dragging your feet; you are guaranteed to end up flush with joy. Maybe that’s part of the point: It changes you inside.

    In a recent development, spencer A. Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin. His new book, A Way With Words: Why Language Makes Humans Irreplaceable, is available for preorder now.

    On “Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity”.

    #134139. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)
